---
title: "5.1 Bernoulli's Equation"
---

{{< include ../_checkpoint-widget.qmd >}}

## The big idea

<!-- We are done holding fluids still. Now they move, and we want to know how pressure, speed, and elevation trade off against one another as a parcel of fluid travels along. The answer is Bernoulli's Equation, and the honest way to describe it is this: it is $\sum F = ma$ applied to a little blob of fluid, integrated along the path that blob follows. Nothing more exotic than that.

The price of admission is that we throw away viscosity. No viscous drag, no dissipation — so whatever mechanical energy the parcel starts with, it keeps, just shuffled between pressure, motion, and height. That sounds like a wild assumption, but the number in charge here is the Reynolds number, and we'll see that in a great many everyday flows $\mathrm{Re}\gg 1$ and viscosity really is a rounding error. -->


## Think first

**Recall**

1. $\sum F = ma$, and that pressure differences across a body produce a net force.
2. Hydrostatics gave us $p=\rho g h$ when nothing moves. What happens to that when things do move?
3. The Reynolds number $\mathrm{Re} = \rho U D/\mu$ compares inertia to viscosity.

**Look ahead**

1. What exactly is a *streamline*, and why does Bernoulli only work along one?
2. If a flow speeds up, does its pressure go up or down? (Answer this before you read on — it's worth being wrong on paper.)
3. If a duct narrows, where does the extra speed come from?

## Streamlines

Bernoulli's Equation applies to fluid parcels along **streamlines**, so let's say what those are first.

> A **streamline** is a line that is everywhere parallel to the velocity vector field.

If you make a quiver (arrow) plot of the velocity field, a streamline is a curve that is always (locally) aligned with those arrows. In steady flow, a streamline is also the path a fluid parcel actually travels. Importantly, this means we can think about that fluid parcel and apply our physics equations to it: conservation of momentum and energy. 

::: {.column-margin}
In unsteady flow we also talk about *pathlines* and *streaklines*, which have subtly different meanings (that you can look up, if interested). The one we are focusing on in 3021 is *streamlines*.
:::

Let's think about this picture:

## Newton's second law along a streamline

<!-- Let's write $\sum F_s = m a_s$ in the streamline direction. Two decisions before we start:

- We will consider **gravity** and the **forces due to pressure differentials**. Those are our only forces.
- We are going to **neglect viscous drag**, $\mu \approx 0$. (This is the assumption that will eventually come back to bite us in pipe flow. For now, enjoy it.)

**The pressure force.** Pressure acts on the front and back faces of the parcel, each of area $A$. If pressure varies along $s$, the two faces don't cancel, and the net force is the *difference*: $-A\frac{\partial p}{\partial s}\Delta s$. The minus sign says the parcel gets pushed from high pressure toward low pressure, which is the only sensible thing for it to do.

**The gravity force.** Only the component of weight along $s$ matters, and that component is $-mg\frac{\partial z}{\partial s}$ — if the streamline climbs ($\partial z/\partial s>0$), gravity pulls backwards along it.

**The acceleration.** Here's the sneaky part. The parcel's speed is $V_s$, and its acceleration is $\partial V_s/\partial t$. But we're following a parcel whose position is $s(t)$, so $V$ is really $V(s(t))$ and the chain rule gives

$$
\frac{\partial V_s}{\partial t} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial s}{\partial t}}_{V_s}\frac{\partial V_s}{\partial s} = V_s \frac{\partial V_s}{\partial s}.
$$

::: {.callout-note}
This chain-rule move is the seed of the **material derivative**, which we'll meet properly later. The idea that "steady flow" does not mean "no acceleration" is one of the genuinely surprising facts in this course: a flow can be perfectly steady in time and still accelerate a parcel, simply because the parcel moves to a place where the speed is different.
:::

Putting the three pieces together:

$$
-A\frac{\partial p}{\partial s}\Delta s \;-\; m g \frac{\partial z}{\partial s} \;=\; m \,V_s \frac{\partial V_s}{\partial s}.
$$

Now notice that $A\Delta s$ is just the parcel's volume, and $m = \rho\,(\text{volume})$. Substituting:

$$
-\,(\text{volume})\frac{\partial p}{\partial s} \;-\; \rho\,(\text{volume})\, g \frac{\partial z}{\partial s} \;=\; \rho\,(\text{volume})\, V_s \frac{\partial V_s}{\partial s}.
$$

Volume divides out of every term. That's a good sign — it means the result is about the fluid, not about how big a blob we happened to draw.

## Integrate along the streamline

Divide by the volume and integrate each term with respect to $s$, following the parcel down its streamline:

$$
\int -\frac{\partial p}{\partial s}\,ds \;-\; \int \rho g \frac{\partial z}{\partial s}\,ds \;=\; \int \rho V \frac{\partial V}{\partial s}\,ds.
$$

Every one of these is a fundamental-theorem-of-calculus freebie. The first two integrands are exact derivatives of $p$ and $z$; the third is the derivative of $\tfrac12 V^2$. Taking $\rho$ and $g$ as constants:

$$
-p - \rho g z = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 - \text{constant}.
$$

Rearrange, and there it is:

::: {.callout-important}
## Bernoulli's Equation

$$
p + \rho g z + \frac{1}{2}\rho V^2 = \text{constant along a streamline}
$$
:::

This is one equation mechanical engineers actually memorize — or at least the principle behind it, the **"Bernoulli Principle"**: a flow that speeds up will *decrease* in pressure. That single sentence explains a startling amount of the world:

- It is the reason for **airfoil lift** (faster over the top, lower pressure over the top).
- **Firefighters** are concerned about this — fast flow past a surface pulls on it.
- **Entrainment**: moving air drags extra air in alongside it, and the low pressure it creates sucks in still more.

### When are we allowed to do this?

We threw away viscosity, so we should check whether that was defensible. The number in charge is the Reynolds number,

$$
\mathrm{Re} = \frac{\rho U D}{\mu},
$$

and an awful lot of applications sit at $\mathrm{Re}\gg 1$. Wave your arm through the air: $U\sim 2$ m/s, $D\sim 0.1$ m, and for air $\rho\approx 1.2$ kg/m³, $\mu\approx 1.8\times10^{-5}$ Pa·s. That's

$$
\mathrm{Re} = \frac{(1.2)(2)(0.1)}{1.8\times 10^{-5}} \approx 10^4,
$$

which is to say viscosity is "small" — inertia beats it by four orders of magnitude. Casually waving your arm around is a high-Reynolds-number flow. Bernoulli is not some exotic limit; it's most of daily life.

## Interpretation of the terms

Step back and look at what we actually did. We took $F = ma$ (per unit volume, really) and integrated it over a distance $ds$. Force times distance is *work*, which means:

- Bernoulli's Equation is **conservation of energy along a streamline**.
- And we assumed **no energy dissipation**, $\mu = 0$, which is exactly why nothing leaks out of the ledger.

So each term is an energy per unit volume:

$$
\underbrace{p}_{\text{flow work}} \;+\; \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2}_{\text{kinetic energy}} \;+\; \underbrace{\rho g z}_{\text{potential energy}} \;=\; \text{constant}.
$$

Check the units if you like: J/m³ is the same thing as Pa. Every term in Bernoulli is a pressure *and* an energy density, simultaneously. That double identity is why the equation is so easy to misuse — the algebra never complains, even when you apply it across two points that aren't on the same streamline, or across a region that dissipates energy.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The misconception to kill now
"Faster flow $\Rightarrow$ lower pressure" is a *consequence* of the constant being constant, not a law of nature. It only holds **along one streamline**, in a **steady**, **inviscid**, **incompressible** flow. Hand a fan and a loose sheet of paper to someone who over-applies it and you will get a confident, wrong prediction. If energy is being added (a pump) or destroyed (friction, a sudden expansion, a shock), Bernoulli is the wrong tool and you want the head equation instead.
::: -->

<!-- For a cross-section over which the velocity is constant, the **mass flow rate** is

$$
\dot{m} = \rho U A, \qquad \left[\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{s}}\right] = \left[\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{m}^3}\right]\left[\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}\right]\left[\text{m}^2\right].
$$

The units work, which is the whole reason to believe the formula. The **volumetric flow rate** is just $Q = \dot{m}/\rho$, in m³/s.

Conservation of mass for this duct says whatever goes in must come out — there's nowhere else for it to go:

$$
\dot{m}_1 = \dot{m}_2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \rho U_1 A_1 = \rho U_2 A_2 \quad (\rho = \text{const})
$$

$$
\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{\;U_2 = U_1 \frac{A_1}{A_2}\;}
$$

Squeeze the area down by a factor of three and the speed goes up by a factor of three. Nothing subtle, but it is the workhorse.

## Putting them together: how does the pressure change?

Now the actual question. Assume $p_1$ is known — how does pressure change from $A_1$ to $A_2$?

Write Bernoulli between a point at station 1 and a point at station 2 on the same streamline:

$$
p_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho U_1^2 + \rho g z_1 \;=\; p_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho U_2^2 + \rho g z_2 .
$$

The duct is horizontal, so $z_1 = z_2$ and those two terms cancel. (More honestly: $z_1 \approx z_2$ — the duct has some height to it, so points across the inlet aren't all at the same elevation. For a duct of this size in water the $\rho g z$ variation is real but small compared to what the velocity terms are doing, and in air it's utterly negligible.)

Substituting $U_2 = U_1 A_1/A_2$ from conservation of mass:

$$
p_2 = p_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho U_1^2\left[1 - \left(\frac{A_1}{A_2}\right)^2\right]
$$

or, written the way you'll more often want it,

::: {.callout-important}
$$
p_1 - p_2 = \frac{1}{2}\rho U_1^{2}\left[\left(\frac{A_1}{A_2}\right)^{2} - 1\right]
$$
:::

Sanity check the physics before trusting it. For a contraction, $A_1 > A_2$, so the bracket is positive and $p_1 > p_2$: the pressure drops as the flow accelerates into the narrow section. That's the Bernoulli Principle doing exactly what it advertised. And if $A_1 = A_2$ — no contraction at all — the bracket vanishes and $p_1 = p_2$, as it must.

Notice also that the pressure drop scales with the *square* of the area ratio. Halve the area and you don't pay double, you pay $4-1=3$ times the inlet dynamic pressure. This is precisely the effect we will weaponize in the next reading to *measure* flow rate: squeeze the pipe, read the pressure drop, back out the speed. That's a venturi meter.

## Earn it — 3 quick gates

Water ($\rho = 1000$ kg/m³) flows through a horizontal contraction. At station 1, $U_1 = 2.0$ m/s. The area shrinks by a factor of three, so $A_1/A_2 = 3$.

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="What is U₂, the speed in the narrow section?"
     data-answer="6" data-tol="0.03" data-units="m/s"
     data-hint="Conservation of mass: U₂ = U₁·(A₁/A₂). Nothing squared here — that comes later."
     data-solution="U₂ = U₁·A₁/A₂ = (2.0)(3) = 6.0 m/s."
     data-target="bern-gate-1"
     data-ok-text="&#10003; yes — three times the area ratio, three times the speed."></div>
```

::: {#bern-gate-1 .fl-hidden}
Six meters per second. Now the pressure drop that goes with it.

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="What is p₁ − p₂, in kPa?"
     data-answer="16" data-tol="0.03" data-units="kPa"
     data-hint="p₁ − p₂ = ½ρU₁²[(A₁/A₂)² − 1]. The bracket is 9 − 1, not 3 − 1."
     data-solution="½(1000)(2.0²)[3² − 1] = (2000)(8) = 16000 Pa = 16 kPa."
     data-target="bern-gate-2"
     data-ok-text="&#10003; correct — 16 kPa, and note it came from 9−1, not 3−1."></div>
```
:::

::: {#bern-gate-2 .fl-hidden}
16 kPa. For scale, that's about a fifth of Boulder's 83 kPa atmosphere — a real pressure drop from a very ordinary-sounding contraction.

One more, to make sure the Reynolds-number licence is more than a slogan. Same water, $U = 2.0$ m/s, pipe diameter $D = 0.05$ m, $\mu = 1.0\times10^{-3}$ Pa·s.

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="What is Re? (Give it in thousands, e.g. enter 42 for 42,000.)"
     data-answer="100" data-tol="0.03" data-units="thousand"
     data-hint="Re = ρUD/μ = (1000)(2.0)(0.05)/(1.0e−3). Then divide by 1000 to report."
     data-solution="Re = (1000)(2.0)(0.05)/(1.0×10⁻³) = 1.0×10⁵ = 100 thousand. Inertia beats viscosity by five orders of magnitude, so dropping μ was fair."
     data-target="bern-gate-3"
     data-ok-text="&#10003; Re = 10⁵ — comfortably in Bernoulli territory."></div>
```
:::

::: {#bern-gate-3 .fl-hidden}
$\mathrm{Re}=10^5$. Viscosity is not zero, but it is nowhere near in charge, and that is the whole justification for everything on this page.
:::

## Check yourself

<details>
<summary>What is a streamline, in one sentence?</summary>
A line that is everywhere parallel to the velocity vector field. In steady flow it is also the path a fluid parcel actually travels.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Which two forces did we include in ∑F<sub>s</sub> = ma<sub>s</sub>, and which did we throw away?</summary>
We kept gravity and the net force from pressure differences along the streamline. We threw away viscous drag by setting μ ≈ 0.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Where did the V ∂V/∂s on the right-hand side come from?</summary>
The chain rule. The parcel's speed is V(s(t)), so ∂V/∂t = (∂s/∂t)(∂V/∂s) = V ∂V/∂s. A steady flow can still accelerate a parcel, because the parcel moves to where the speed is different.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Why did the parcel's volume disappear from the equation?</summary>
Every term carried a factor of A·Δs (the volume), so it divided out. The result is a statement about the fluid, not about the size of blob we chose to draw.
</details>

<details>
<summary>What does each of p, ½ρV², and ρgz represent physically, and what are their units?</summary>
Flow work, kinetic energy, and potential energy — all per unit volume. The units are J/m³, which is identical to Pa. Every Bernoulli term is simultaneously a pressure and an energy density.
</details>

<details>
<summary>A duct's area doubles. What happens to the speed, and what happens to the pressure?</summary>
U₂ = U₁(A₁/A₂) = U₁/2, so the flow slows down, and by Bernoulli the pressure rises: p₁ − p₂ = ½ρU₁²[(1/2)² − 1] = −(3/8)ρU₁², i.e. p₂ > p₁.
</details>
